documents.title: Association of British Neurologists revised guidelines for prescribing disease modifying treatments MS

chunks.content: Introduction Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune disorder of the central nervous system (CNS) involving inflammatory demyelination, gliosis, and progressive neuronal loss. The disease manifests as a wide spectrum of neurological symptoms, including visual impairment, sensory disturbances, motor weakness, and cognitive decline. These symptoms vary according to the location of CNS lesions (Noyes and Weinstock-Guttman ). The disease process is characterized by perivascular lymphocytic infiltration and macrophage-mediated degradation of the myelin sheath. Clinically, MS is traditionally classified into distinct phenotypes. Approximately 85% of patients present with relapsing-remitting MS (RRMS), while about 15% exhibit progressive disability from the onset, known as primary progressive MS (PPMS). A significant majority of RRMS patients eventually transition to secondary progressive MS (SPMS), with age being the predominant predictor of this progression (University of California et al. 2016; Zawadzka et al. ). However, the traditional clinical classification is increasingly viewed as insufficient for capturing the disease’s full biological heterogeneity. Contemporary research advocates a more dynamic, mechanism-based framework integrating underlying pathological processes, such as inflammatory activity, neurodegeneration, and cortical pathology, alongside clinical metrics (University of California et al. 2016; Amin and Hersh ). For example, the concept of progression independent of relapse activity (PIRA) and the use of advanced MRI biomarkers, such as cortical lesion volume and spinal cord atrophy, are now recognized as more reliable indicators of disease severity and accumulation of disability across all subtypes (University of California et al. 2016; Amin and Hersh ). This evolving understanding highlights the importance of a multidimensional approach to assessing diseases and personalizing treatments. The clinical management of MS currently relies on a growing repertoire of disease-modifying therapies, including corticosteroids, immunosuppressants, and more targeted agents, such as interferon-β and glatiramer acetate. These treatments primarily modulate immune cell activity, and they are most effective at reducing relapse frequency and delaying the accumulation of disability when initiated early in the relapsing phase of the disease (Scolding et al. ; Brown et al. ; Montalban et al. ). Despite these advances, significant therapeutic limitations persist. Current agents are largely ineffective at promoting repair, and they are less effective in progressive forms of the disease. The modest benefits of a few agents, such as ocrelizumab for PPMS, underscore the urgent need for neuroprotective and regenerative strategies (Hauser et al. ; Rasband and Peles ). Central to the pathology of MS is the loss of myelin, a specialized electrical insulator that is essential for normal neuronal function (Sampaio-Baptista and Johansen-Berg ). Oligodendrocytes, which produce myelin in the CNS, continuously remodel sheaths in an activity-dependent manner. This process plays a crucial role in neural plasticity and learning (Akay et al. ). These cells develop from oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPCs), which are distributed throughout the brain and receive direct synaptic input from neurons (Liu et al. ). The process by which OPCs differentiate into mature, myelinating oligodendrocytes is complex and involves an intricate interplay of extracellular signals, intrinsic molecular machinery, and epigenetic regulation (Zhou et al. ). Within this regulatory framework, microRNAs (miRNAs) have emerged as key post-transcriptional regulators. These small, non-coding RNAs typically suppress gene expression by destabilizing messenger RNA (mRNA) or inhibiting translation. They are implicated in a wide range of pathologies, including neurodegenerative diseases (Wang et al. , b). In the context of MS, two miRNAs are of particular interest: miR-219 and miR-146a. miR-219 has been shown to play a critical role in promoting oligodendrocyte differentiation and remyelination. Its therapeutic potential has been demonstrated through enhanced myelin repair in animal models following its augmentation (Tahamtan et al. ). On the other hand, miRNA-146a is associated with MS susceptibility and inflammatory activity. It shows significant dysregulation in active lesions and represents a plausible therapeutic target for modulating the immune response (Li et al. ; Franklin and Ffrench-Constant ). Since current MS therapeutics cannot repair existing demyelination, emerging research is intensely focused on remyelination as a promising way to stop the progression of disability (Fünfschilling et al. ). This focus is bolstered by the understanding that myelin sheaths and oligodendrocytes provide crucial neuroprotective support to axons and that their loss contributes directly to irreversible neurodegeneration (Morrison et al. ). Thus, this review will examine the therapeutic potential of targeting miRNAs, specifically the roles of miR-219 in promoting myelin repair and of miR-146a in controlling inflammation, as a novel approach for treating MS. Multiple Sclerosis Pathology: A Dual Demyelination-Inflammation Paradigm Myelination is an evolutionarily optimized mechanism for neural conduction that significantly enhances the efficiency of nerve impulse propagation. This specialized structure increases the transverse resistance of the axon membrane and concentrates voltage-gated ion channels at the nodes of Ranvier. This enables the rapid, energy-efficient saltatory conduction of action potentials (Nave and Werner ). The consequences of demyelination extend beyond slowed conduction to include complete conduction block, which highlights the critical importance of remyelination for restoring normal neurological function. Notably, successful remyelination has been shown to correlate with clinical functional recovery in animal models and human studies (Duncan et al. ). The relationship between oligodendrocytes and axons is much more complex than simple electrical insulation Consistent neuropathological evidence shows that remyelinated axons have significantly greater resistance to degeneration than chronically demyelinated fibers. This establishes remyelination as a dual-purpose therapeutic strategy that targets functional recovery and long-term neuroprotection (Mei et al. ). Recent research has revealed that myelin regulation is an ongoing, dynamic process in which newly formed and existing oligodendrocytes continuously remodel myelin in response to neural activity. This process plays a crucial role in learning and neural plasticity (Sampaio-Baptista and Johansen-Berg ). Clinical observations demonstrate substantial variability in endogenous remyelination capacity among MS patients, yet this is insufficient. Histopathological studies have documented cases of extensive remyelination, even in patients with long-standing MS, while others show markedly limited repair capacity. Advanced neuroimaging techniques, particularly myelin-sensitive PET tracers, have confirmed these findings in vivo, revealing patterns of myelin repair that inversely correlate with clinical disability measures. These imaging studies have been instrumental in establishing the relationship between remyelination capacity and clinical outcomes, thereby reinforcing the therapeutic potential of enhancing this natural repair process (Bodini et al. ; Bramow et al. ). At the cellular level, remyelination depends largely on the activation and differentiation of adult OPCs. These progenitor cells are derived from neonatal precursors and maintain their population primarily through self-renewal rather than recruitment from neural stem cell niches (Zawadzka et al. ). Following demyelinating injury, adult OPCs undergo a precisely coordinated sequence of activation, proliferation, migration, and differentiation to generate new myelin sheaths (Xia and Fancy ). The failure of remyelination in MS likely results from complex interactions between multiple pathological mechanisms (Hammond et al. ). The presence of undifferentiated adult OPCs in chronic lesions suggests an impaired differentiation capacity (Liddelow et al. ). These findings have significantly influenced therapeutic development, shifting the focus toward combination strategies that target OPC differentiation pathways and modulate the inhibitory lesion environment simultaneously (He et al. ; Duncan et al. ). Oligodendrocyte Lineage and Dynamic Myelination in Health and MS The oligodendrocyte lineage is essential for the structure and function of the CNS, comprising OPCs and their mature counterparts, myelinating oligodendrocytes. OPCs are characterized by the expression of markers such as PDGFR-α and NG2. They constitute a significant and persistent progenitor population, accounting for approximately 5–10% of total brain cells throughout life (Fernandez-Castaneda and Gaultier ; Bonora et al. ; Beiter et al. ). During development, these cells proliferate and migrate from the ventricular zone; their identity is marked by transcription factors such as Olig2 and Sox10 (Falcão et al. ). In a healthy adult CNS, OPCs are among the most actively dividing cell types. They are widely distributed and poised to fulfill their primary role of generating new myelinating oligodendrocytes (Wang et al. ). In addition to their regenerative capacity, OPCs play an essential role in brain physiology by receiving direct synaptic input from neurons and contributing to the maintenance of the blood-brain barrier (BBB) (Chamberlain et al. ). The transition from a proliferative OPC to a mature, myelinating oligodendrocyte is a precisely orchestrated, multi-stage process. This differentiation involves cell cycle exit, profound morphological transformation, and molecular maturation. These processes are driven by the integration of intrinsic developmental programs and extrinsic environmental signals (Bergles and Richardson ; Sock and Wegner ). Neural activity itself is a critical regulator of this process, driving activity-dependent myelination. This mechanism is a fundamental form of neural network adaptation that is essential for higher-order cognitive functions, including learning (Gibson et al. ; Bacmeister et al. ). The differentiation program is governed by complex regulatory networks that translate environmental cues into coordinated gene expression. Epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, and microRNA networks, act as molecular switches that activate the transcriptional machinery necessary for progression through the lineage and acquisition of myelination competence Various inhibitory factors in the extracellular environment can disrupt this process, including specific extracellular matrix components (e.g., LINGO-1 and glycosaminoglycans) and secreted signaling molecules (e.g., BMPs and FGFs), which interfere with critical transcriptional and epigenetic machinery (Wheeler and Fuss ).

Epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation, histone modifications, and microRNA networks, act as molecular switches that activate the transcriptional machinery necessary for progression through the lineage and acquisition of myelination competence Various inhibitory factors in the extracellular environment can disrupt this process, including specific extracellular matrix components (e.g., LINGO-1 and glycosaminoglycans) and secreted signaling molecules (e.g., BMPs and FGFs), which interfere with critical transcriptional and epigenetic machinery (Wheeler and Fuss ). In MS, this regulated lineage is profoundly disrupted, resulting in failed remyelination and progressive neurodegeneration (Stys and Tsutsui ). Following a demyelinating injury, OPCs are activated, proliferate, and migrate to lesion sites to initiate repair (Tepavčević and Lubetzki ). However, in the context of MS, this regenerative process is often incomplete. A complex interplay of cell-intrinsic and extrinsic inhibitory factors prevents OPCs from maturing into functional, myelinating oligodendrocytes. This results in persistent demyelination within chronic lesions (Gharagozloo et al. ). Intrinsically, a differentiation blockade is established through epigenetic modifications, such as repressive histone marks (e.g., H3K27me3), as well as the dysregulation of key master transcription factors, such as MYRF and SOX10, which are necessary for the expression of myelin genes (Tiane et al. ). The inflammatory milieu of the MS lesion is a major extrinsic deterrent. Pro-inflammatory cytokines, including interferon gamma (IFN-γ) and TNF-α, signal through pathways such as STAT1 and NF-κB, which actively inhibit OPC maturation. These cytokines can even reprogram OPCs toward immunogenic phenotypes (Brambilla et al. ). Additionally, altered extracellular matrix components in lesions, such as chondroitin sulfate proteoglycans and hyaluronan, engage receptors on OPCs and activate inhibitory signaling cascades, including RhoA/ROCK. These cascades disrupt the cytoskeletal dynamics essential for morphological differentiation and the extension of myelin membranes required for effective wrapping of axons (Lang et al. ). The convergence of these powerful inhibitory signals within the MS lesion microenvironment ultimately leads to remyelination failure, leaving axons vulnerable to degeneration and contributing to irreversible neurological decline (Zveik et al. ). Neuroimmune Crosstalk in Multiple Sclerosis Remarkable functional parallels exist between the nervous and immune systems, including their sophisticated information processing capabilities, memory formation mechanisms, and finely balanced regulatory networks (Morimoto and Nakajima ). The immune components, including dendritic cells, lymphocytes, and macrophages, play a role in normal neural function and homeostasis, influencing processes ranging from synaptic plasticity to neuronal circuit formation (Derecki et al. ). Molecular mediators of neuroimmune crosstalk operate at multiple levels. Innate immune molecules, including cytokines, toll-like receptors, and complement components, are constitutively expressed in the CNS, where they contribute to brain development and neural connectivity (Lazarczyk et al. ). Pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as IL-6 and TNF-α, serve as both immune messengers and neuromodulators and have been shown to affect synaptic plasticity, learning, and memory processes (Besedovsky and Rey ; He et al. ). Conversely, neurotransmitters, such as acetylcholine, dopamine, and norepinephrine, regulate immune cell function via specific receptors on lymphocytes and antigen-presenting cells (Prado et al. ). Specialized neuroimmune regulatory mechanisms maintain homeostasis in the CNS microenvironment. Neurons and glia constitutively express immunomodulatory factors that suppress excessive microglial activation. Meanwhile, suppressor of cytokine signaling molecules provide negative feedback to prevent cytokine overactivity (Cramer et al. ). This neurogenic modulation of immunity is exemplified by the inflammatory reflex, a neural circuit that helps maintain immune homeostasis (Huston ). Chemokine receptors are another shared signaling system expressed by neural and immune cells that participate in processes ranging from brain development to neuroinflammation. MicroRNAs, such as miR-146a, further integrate these systems by regulating inflammatory responses in both types of cells, demonstrating the molecular complexity of neuroimmune interactions. These multifaceted communication pathways highlight the profound interdependence of the nervous and immune systems in health and disease (Martin et al. ). The Current Therapeutic Landscape in MS: Limitations and Unmet Needs MS is characterized by two interconnected pathological processes: inflammation and neurodegeneration. The disease process often begins with the abnormal activation of autoreactive lymphocytes that target CNS antigens in genetically susceptible individuals. These activated immune cells then proliferate, cross the BBB, and initiate a destructive inflammatory cascade within the CNS. This leads to demyelination and axonal injury, which activates resident microglia. Microglia then release pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, which further amplify the damage by recruiting additional immune cells, including B and T lymphocytes, dendritic cells, and monocytes. This creates a self-perpetuating cycle of inflammation, demyelination, and progressive neuronal loss (Zabalza et al. ). The management of MS has been transformed by the introduction of disease-modifying therapies (DMTs), which are classified by their mechanism and potency. The therapeutic arsenal includes foundational agents, such as interferon formulations and glatiramer acetate; intermediate options, such as S1P receptor modulators; and high-potency treatments,

Microglia then release pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines, which further amplify the damage by recruiting additional immune cells, including B and T lymphocytes, dendritic cells, and monocytes. This creates a self-perpetuating cycle of inflammation, demyelination, and progressive neuronal loss (Zabalza et al. ). The management of MS has been transformed by the introduction of disease-modifying therapies (DMTs), which are classified by their mechanism and potency. The therapeutic arsenal includes foundational agents, such as interferon formulations and glatiramer acetate; intermediate options, such as S1P receptor modulators; and high-potency treatments, including monoclonal antibodies (Jakimovski et al. ; Selmaj et al. ; Florou et al. ). A significant paradigm shift has been the approval of B-cell-depleting agents for progressive forms of MS, offering a treatment option where few existed before (Rae-Grant et al. ). These immunotherapeutic agents are most effective at controlling relapses and delaying the accumulation of disability when initiated early in the disease course. Thus, timely intervention has become a cornerstone of modern MS care (Cobo-Calvo et al. ). Despite these advances, the therapeutic landscape is marked by significant limitations and unmet needs. A primary challenge is the variable efficacy of DMTs across different disease stages and patient subtypes. While they are effective against the inflammatory component of relapsing-remitting MS, many therapies demonstrate limited benefit in halting the progressive, neurodegenerative phase of the disease (Comi et al. ; Franklin and Goldman ). Furthermore, MS heterogeneity means treatment response varies significantly among individuals. A critical lack of predictive biomarkers complicates personalized therapy selection and contributes to therapeutic inertia, or the delay in escalating treatment despite evidence of disease activity (Lassmann ; Rodrigues et al. ). Safety and tolerability concerns also present major hurdles. Many DMTs, particularly immunosuppressive agents, are associated with long-term risks, including serious infections, infusion reactions, and an elevated risk of malignancies, such as progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy which has been associated with natalizumab use (Kuhlmann et al. ; Bayounis et al. ; Sirbu et al. ). The long-term safety profiles of newer, highly effective DMTs are not fully understood, requiring ongoing pharmacovigilance. These risks underscore the need for improved, standardized screening protocols and more consistent patient education regarding potential adverse events (Bayounis et al. ). Beyond managing inflammation, there is a fundamental unmet need for treatments that promote remyelination and repair existing neural damage. Current strategies primarily suppress the immune system, failing to address the restoration of lost neurological function. This underscores the urgent need for neuroprotective and regenerative therapies (Franklin and Goldman ). Finally, the high cost of many DMTs and accessibility issues create economic barriers to optimal care, emphasizing the need for more affordable and inclusive treatment strategies (Attwood et al. ). In conclusion, although the current therapeutic arsenal for MS has considerably improved patient outcomes, there is still much work to be done. Future progress hinges on clarifying the molecular interplay between degeneration and repair, devising targeted neuroprotective strategies, and establishing a more personalized, accessible, and comprehensive approach to patient care (Khan et al. ; Kaufmann et al. ). Drug Targets Under Investigation for Remyelination in MS A diverse array of pharmacological agents and therapeutic strategies aimed at promoting remyelination in MS are currently under investigation in preclinical and clinical studies. These efforts primarily focus on enhancing the differentiation and maturation of OPCs into myelinating oligodendrocytes to restore the protective myelin sheath around axons. Several small-molecule drugs targeting specific receptors and pathways to stimulate this repair process have advanced into clinical trials. Anti-muscarinergic agents, such as clemastine, have demonstrated remyelinating effects by promoting OPC differentiation in animal models such as those exposed to lysolecithin or cuprizone. These results were translated into a phase II trial, in which clemastine significantly reduced visual evoked potential (VEP) latency delays and improved myelin water fraction, indicating renewed myelin integrity (Green et al. ). Similarly, erythropoietin has been shown to promote oligodendrocyte differentiation. Phase II studies in patients with optic neuritis have reported shortened VEP latencies (Heidari et al. ). Other receptor-targeted approaches include histamine H3 receptor antagonists, such as GSK239512, which facilitate OPC differentiation. These antagonists have shown a positive effect on the magnetization transfer ratio in a phase II trial (Chen et al. ). Another approach involves modulating thyroid hormone signaling using agents like sobetirome. Sobetirome has demonstrated remyelinating potential in preclinical models and has been shown to be safe in the short term in an MS phase I trial (Wooliscroft et al. ). Some candidates have faced challenges, such as opicinumab (anti-LINGO-1), which yielded mixed results in Phase II trials, despite promising preclinical data. However, investigation continues in ongoing studies, such as AFFINITY (Cadavid et al. , ). Other promising agents in the pipeline include bazedoxifene, gold nanocrystals (CNM-Au8), and the NMDA receptor antagonist ifenprodil. These agents are being evaluated in clinical trials for their pro-remyelinating potential (Lubetzki et al. ; Rankin et al. ). Beyond conventional pharmacology, significant research is dedicated to harnessing the therapeutic potential of mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and their derivatives. One key approach is to use the MSC secretome, which is the conditioned medium and extracellular vesicles (EVs) that are rich in growth factors, cytokines, and microRNAs. For example, hepatocyte growth factor (HGF), which is secreted by MSCs, has been identified as a critical mediator. Depleting HGF from the MSC secretome blocked functional recovery in an experimental autoimmune encephalomyelitis (EAE) model, while HGF alone was sufficient to promote oligodendrocyte differentiation and remyelination (Bai et al. ). Additionally, miRNAs packaged within MSC-derived EVs, such as miR-367-3p, have been shown to suppress microglial ferroptosis and prevent demyelination by activating the ferroptosis inhibitor glutathione peroxidase 4 (Fan et al. ). Another strategy is to engineer MSCs to overexpress therapeutic genes such as interferon-β (IFN-β) or sphingosine kinase 1. This results in enhanced immunomodulation, improved homing to CNS lesions, and superior remyelination in experimental models compared to native MSCs (Marin-Bañasco et al. ; Wang et al. ). Combining MSCs with other compounds, such as methylprednisolone or resveratrol, has also demonstrated synergistic effects in promoting repair (Kim et al. ). An indirect yet crucial remyelination strategy is to modulate the CNS environment, particularly by influencing the phenotype of microglia. It is essential to shift microglia from a pro-inflammatory (M1) state to a pro-regenerative (M2) state to create an environment conducive to repair. M2 microglia clear inhibitory myelin debris and release supportive factors. The MSC secretome, through factors like TSG-6, has been demonstrated to promote this beneficial M2 polarization (Liu et al. , ). Preconditioning strategies for MSCs, such as exposure to hypoxia or priming with IFN-γ, are being explored to further enhance the secretion of these pro-remyelinating factors (Zhou et al. ). The remyelination therapy landscape is expanding rapidly to encompass direct OPC-targeting drugs, sophisticated cell-based therapies, and innovative approaches to modulate the lesion environment. These multifaceted strategies are progressing from preclinical models to early-phase clinical trials and hold significant promise for achieving the long-sought goal of reversing disability in MS patients. MicroRNAs as Master Regulators of CNS Repair and Inflammation MicroRNAs are a fundamental class of small, non-coding RNA molecules that function as master regulators of gene expression. They orchestrate a wide spectrum of biological processes, including cellular differentiation and immune modulation (Walton et al. ; Desvignes et al. ). In the context of neuroinflammatory disorders, miRNAs have emerged as critical molecular modulators operating at the interface between immune activation and neural repair (Bartel ; O’Brien et al. ). Specific miRNA expression signatures regulate various aspects of neuroinflammation, such as immune cell activation, cytokine production, glial reactivity, and BBB integrity. Concurrently, specialized miRNA networks govern essential processes for neural maintenance, particularly the proliferation and differentiation of OPCs and their capacity for myelination (Pogue and Lukiw ). This dual regulatory capacity establishes miRNAs as pivotal mediators that can influence both inflammatory pathways and endogenous regenerative processes in neurological diseases such as MS (Li et al. ). Multiple sclerosis is a compelling example of the pathological consequences of dysregulated miRNA networks. Specific miRNAs, such as miR-219 and miR-146a, play coordinated yet distinct roles in this disease. For instance, miR-219 promotes oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelination by repressing multiple inhibitory pathways in precursor cells. Its downregulation in chronic MS lesions is a key factor in remyelination failure and disease progression (Hudish et al. ). Conversely, miR-146a is a critical regulator of neuroinflammatory responses. It modulates glial cell activation and pro-inflammatory cytokine production by affecting NF-κB signaling and other inflammatory cascades (Iyer et al. ). The simultaneous dysregulation of these networks creates a compounded pathological environment that perpetuates inflammatory tissue damage while impairing the brain’s intrinsic repair mechanisms (Fig. ). This sophisticated understanding has stimulated the investigation of innovative miRNA-based therapeutic strategies. Recent preclinical studies have significantly elucidated the therapeutic potential of these molecules. For example, Kornfeld et al. demonstrated that overexpressing miR-219 robustly enhances remyelination in chronic demyelination models by promoting oligodendrocyte differentiation and functional recovery. This finding reinforces the status of miR-219 as a master regulator of myelin repair

For example, Kornfeld et al. demonstrated that overexpressing miR-219 robustly enhances remyelination in chronic demyelination models by promoting oligodendrocyte differentiation and functional recovery. This finding reinforces the status of miR-219 as a master regulator of myelin repair (Kornfeld et al. ). Similarly, the immunomodulatory role of miR-146a has been further defined. Zhang et al. reported that administering miR-146a mimics to EAE mice improved clinical scores and increased OPC differentiation by suppressing the Toll-like receptor (TLR2)/Interleukin receptor-associated kinase 1 (IRAK1) pathway (Zhang et al. ). Advances in the field include the development of more physiologically relevant human models, such as immunocompetent cerebral organoids containing microglia and oligodendrocytes. For example, Fagiani et al. used these organoids to recreate MS-specific glial-immune interactions and showed that miR-219 enhances OPC maturation (Fagiani et al. ). Additionally, Silver et al. identified EV-associated miRNAs, including miR-219, that are released by these organoids. This suggests a novel mechanism of intercellular communication that supports remyelination (Silver et al. ). These findings highlight the powerful synergy between miRNA therapeutics and advanced human model systems in developing reparative strategies for MS. Concurrently targeting miRNAs such as miR-219 to promote regeneration and miR-146a to control inflammation is a promising dual-pronged approach to addressing the disease’s complex pathology. miR-219: A Master Regulator of Oligodendrogenesis and Remyelination Within the CNS, miR-219 acts as a master orchestrator, creating a microenvironment conducive to repair. It does so by directly promoting oligodendrocyte differentiation and simultaneously mitigating multiple inhibitory processes. Its therapeutic influence extends beyond a single pathway, exerting comprehensive modulatory effects on the cellular and metabolic landscape. A key aspect of its function is the suppression of reactive astrogliosis by directly downregulating glial fibrillary acidic protein. This helps mitigate the formation of inhibitory glial scars, which are a major impediment to axonal regeneration in demyelinating conditions such as MS (Nguyen et al. ). Additionally, miR-219 targets the neuroepithelial stem cell protein NESTIN, whose pathological overexpression in reactive astrocytes is strongly correlated with the formation of inflammatory lesions in MS patients (Nazari et al. ). At the metabolic level, miR-219 provides additional protection by inhibiting the elongation of very long-chain fatty acids. This prevents the accumulation of membrane-destabilizing lipids that contribute to oxidative damage, inflammation, and subsequent demyelination (Li and Yao ) (Fig. ). The pro-myelinating effect of miR-219 has been significantly validated in complex human model systems. Research utilizing human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived oligodendrocyte progenitor cells has confirmed that overexpressing miR-219 accelerates their differentiation into mature, myelinating oligodendrocytes. This accelerated maturation is driven by direct repression of key inhibitory targets, such as LINGO-1 and ETV5. This provides crucial, human-centric evidence of its therapeutic role (Shamaeizadeh and Mirian ). Furthermore, the scope of miR-219’s activity includes the beneficial modulation of the neuroinflammatory environment. One study using the EAE model showed that miR-219-5p drives oligodendrocyte differentiation and influences microglial activation, shifting it toward a more reparative phenotype. This dual action reduces the overall inflammatory burden and creates a more favorable environment for remyelination (Maciak et al. ). Recent investigations have advanced our understanding of the therapeutic potential of miR-219 from foundational concepts to validated delivery strategies. A pivotal study demonstrated that an miR-219a-5p mimic encapsulated within a sophisticated, glutathione-targeted, tragacanthic acid-chitosan nanoparticle system could effectively cross the BBB via intranasal delivery. This targeted approach promoted robust remyelination and significantly improved clinical scores in a cuprizone-induced demyelination model. These results highlight a novel, efficient delivery strategy for translating miR-219-based therapeutics into clinical practice (Silver et al. ). Molecular Mechanisms of miR-219 in Oligodendrocyte Differentiation Oligodendrocytes are the primary myelinating cells of the CNS. These glial cells are essential for the proper development and function of the CNS. Dysfunction or damage to these cells has been linked to various neurological disorders, including MS, traumatic brain injuries, and cerebrovascular accidents (Zhao et al. ). Recent studies have identified -miR-219 as a key regulator of oligodendrocyte differentiation and myelination. Clinical studies have shown that healthy individuals have significantly higher expression levels of miR-219 than patients with progressive forms of MS. This suggests that it could be useful as a diagnostic biomarker (Dugas et al. ). This suggests that it could be useful as a diagnostic biomarker (Dugas et al. ). The molecular mechanisms by which miR-219 promotes oligodendrocyte lineage progression involve sophisticated regulatory networks. This microRNA orchestrates the critical transition of OPCs from proliferative, self-renewing states to differentiation-competent states by simultaneously targeting multiple inhibitory pathways These pathways include platelet-derived growth factor receptor alpha (PDGFRα), HES5, SOX6, FOXJ3, and ETV5, which are all well-established negative regulators of oligodendrocyte differentiation and maintain OPCs in a proliferative state when overexpressed. Furthermore, miR-219 enhances the myelination program by upregulating monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1) expression and suppressing differentiation inhibitors, such as SOX6 and HES5. Pharmacological studies have demonstrated that MCT1 inhibition reduces both the number of oligodendrocytes and myelin basic protein levels (Liu et al. , ). The considerable therapeutic potential of miR-219 is highlighted by its ability to coordinately regulate multiple critical aspects of oligodendrocyte biology and function. Experimental administration of miR-219 has been shown to significantly increase the expression of mature oligodendrocyte markers (CNP, MBP, and MAG), while simultaneously suppressing the expression of OPC markers (PDGFRα and NG2) and indicators of astrocytic activation (Nguyen et al. ; Shamaeizadeh and Mirian ). It maintains essential myelin homeostasis by balancing the expression of neuroprotective proteins and suppressing neurogenic factors that could divert OPCs from their proper differentiation pathway. These comprehensive, multifaceted regulatory actions firmly establish miR-219 as a master controller of CNS myelination processes and a highly promising therapeutic target for various demyelinating disorders (Shamaeizadeh and Mirian ; Varma-Doyle et al. ) (Fig. ). Dysregulation of miR-219 and Remyelination Failure in MS Persistent failure of remyelination is a fundamental pathological feature of MS and a major contributor to progressive neurological disability. This failure to repair does not stem from an absence of OPCs, which are often present in MS lesions. Rather, it stems from a disruption of the complex signaling process required for OPCs to differentiate into mature, myelinating oligodendrocytes (Galloway et al. ; Franklin and Gallo ). One key factor in this failure is the pathological dysregulation of miR-219, a molecule that is now recognized as a central orchestrator of myelin repair. The miR-219 is highly and specifically expressed during the normal differentiation of OPCs into mature oligodendrocytes, a process essential for myelination and repair in the CNS (Shamaeizadeh and Mirian ). The critical role of miR-219 is underscored by the severe myelination defects observed when global microRNA processing is disrupted (Dugas et al. ). However, in the context of MS, this vital molecule is significantly downregulated. This deficiency is evident in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of patients with progressive forms of MS and is notably absent within chronic MS lesions (Shamaeizadeh and Mirian ; Dugas et al. ; Junker et al. ). This loss creates a molecular environment hostile to repair; miR-219 normally promotes oligodendrocyte differentiation by repressing a network of key inhibitors, including PDGFRα, SOX6, HES5, and LINGO1 (Akay et al. ; Zhao et al. ; Dugas et al. ). When miR-219 levels fall, these inhibitory proteins accumulate and block the transition of OPCs from a proliferative state to a mature, myelinating state. Furthermore, miR-219 directly promotes the expression of essential myelin-related genes, such as MBP, PLP, and MAG, which are necessary for constructing and maintaining the myelin sheath (Suster and Feng ). Impairment of remyelination in MS is further exacerbated by multiple inhibitory signaling pathways, including bone morphogenetic protein (BMP), Notch, Wnt, and LINGO1. These pathways converge to create a powerful barrier to OPC differentiation (Gallo and Deneen ; Sabo et al. ). The downregulation of miR-219 appears to be both a cause and a consequence of this hostile environment. The inflammatory environment characteristic of active MS lesions suppresses miR-219 expression, creating a vicious cycle in which inflammatory damage inhibits the molecular machinery necessary for repair (Wang et al. , b). Experimental evidence strongly supports the therapeutic potential of restoring miR-219. Overexpression of miR-219 in models of demyelination consistently enhances oligodendrocyte differentiation and drives remyelination. In contrast, inhibition of miR-219 exacerbates demyelination and impairs functional recovery (Ling et al. ). miR-146a: A Pivotal Modulator of Neuroinflammation MiR-146a has emerged as a critical regulator in the CNS, demonstrating significant dysregulation across various neurological conditions and disease stages (Ma et al. ). This miRNA is involved in many major neurological disorders, including cerebrovascular diseases, traumatic CNS injuries, neurodegenerative conditions, neuroautoimmune disorders, viral infections of the nervous system, peripheral neuropathies, and neurological tumors (He et al. ). Distinct and Shared Functions of miR-146a and miR-146b in MS In MS, miR-146a and miR-146b exhibit a complex interplay of cooperative and divergent functions within the neuroinflammatory landscape. These miRNAs are often overexpressed in critical areas of MS pathology, such as the CSF of patients with active gadolinium-enhancing lesions, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), and brain white matter lesions. They are also present in the EAE mouse model (Confavreux et al. ; Lescher et al. ). This co-upregulation suggests their shared involvement in the immunopathology of the disease. They act as critical negative feedback regulators of the innate immune response by targeting and suppressing key signaling molecules in the interleukin-1 receptor (IL-1R) and TLR pathways. The most notable of these are IRAK1 and TNF receptor-associated factor 6 (TRAF6) (Confavreux et al. ; Mendell and Olson ; Frohman et al. ; Moraghebi et al. ). Suppressing IRAK1 is particularly significant because IRAK1-deficient models are resistant to EAE, which highlights the pro-inflammatory role of this pathway (Ling et al. ). Pathway analyses confirm that their collective target genes are heavily involved in fundamental processes such as apoptosis, cell migration, proliferation, and cytokine-mediated signaling, all of which are central to MS pathogenesis (Confavreux et al. ; Rovira et al. ). Despite their significant similarities, which are driven by an identical seed sequence that predicts overlapping target genes, the two isoforms are not functionally redundant. Their differences stem from their distinct genomic locations miR-146a is located on chromosome 5, while miR-146b is located on chromosome 10 and variations in their transcriptional regulation (Moraghebi et al. ; Paterson and Kriegel ). These differences result in context-specific expression patterns. For example, miR-146a is strongly induced by IL-1β, while miR-146b expression is more responsive to IFN-γ (Otaegui et al. ). These regulatory differences can result in one being upregulated while the other is downregulated in certain pathological conditions, which highlights their non-redundant roles (Paterson and Kriegel ). This divergence is further evidenced by their distinct effects on immune responses in MS. miR-146a has been shown to promote neuroinflammation by enhancing IL-17 production and contributing to T helper 17 cell differentiation by inhibiting IRAK1 (Xia et al. ). Conversely, miR-146b appears to have more anti-inflammatory effects, such as activating the NF-κB pathway and suppressing the production of proinflammatory cytokines and chemokines (Nata et al. ). Thus, there is a nuanced dynamic in which miR-146a enhances inflammatory T-cell responses while miR-146b tempers excessive inflammation (Ma et al. ). Furthermore, genetic variations contribute to their distinct clinical associations. The single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) rs2910164 in the seed region of miR-146a is strongly associated with altered expression and MS susceptibility. In contrast, polymorphisms in miR-146b, such as rs944564808, affect its stability and function, and may correlate with different clinical outcomes (Moraghebi et al. ). A thorough understanding of these subtle yet important distinctions is essential for unraveling their precise contributions to MS mechanisms and considering them as separate entities in future therapeutic strategies. The Role of miR-146a in Regulating Innate and Adaptive Immunity The miR-146a is a critical negative feedback regulator within the immune system. It primarily functions to prevent excessive inflammatory responses by targeting and suppressing key signaling molecules in the NF-κB pathway, such as IRAK1 and TRAF6 (Marino et al. ). Pro-inflammatory stimuli like TNF-α and IL-1 strongly induce its expression, and its dysregulation is a hallmark of autoimmune pathologies, including MS and its EAE model. During the acute phase of EAE, elevated levels of miR-146a are present in peripheral immune tissues, suggesting its involvement in the initial inflammatory surge. However, its expression declines in the chronic phase, indicating a potential failure of this regulatory mechanism over time (Gharibi et al. ). This dynamic expression pattern highlights a paradox: although miR-146a is an inflammation suppressor, its sustained elevation in autoimmunity may indicate an inadequate feedback loop that cannot fully restrain persistent immune activation (Aslani et al. ). The role of miR-146a in the CNS during demyelination and remyelination reveals context-dependent and biphasic functionality (Slota and Booth ). During active demyelination, the genetic deletion of miR-146a leads to decreased macrophage infiltration and an attenuated inflammatory response. Paradoxically, this anti-inflammatory state coincides with an increased number of mature, myelinating oligodendrocytes, which suggests that miR-146a may contribute to inflammation-mediated damage during this phase (Martin et al. ). In contrast, during the subsequent repair phase, mice deficient in miR-146a exhibit impaired recruitment and differentiation

During active demyelination, the genetic deletion of miR-146a leads to decreased macrophage infiltration and an attenuated inflammatory response. Paradoxically, this anti-inflammatory state coincides with an increased number of mature, myelinating oligodendrocytes, which suggests that miR-146a may contribute to inflammation-mediated damage during this phase (Martin et al. ). In contrast, during the subsequent repair phase, mice deficient in miR-146a exhibit impaired recruitment and differentiation of OPCs, indicating a critical pro-regenerative function of the microRNA in remyelination (Martin et al. ). Therapeutic studies further corroborate this biphasic nature. Administration of miR-146a mimics in relapsing-remitting models enhances the differentiation of myelinating oligodendrocytes and promotes anti-inflammatory M2 macrophage polarization. These pro-remyelination effects are mediated by suppression of the TLR2/IRAK1/TRAF6/NF-κB signaling axis (Zhang et al. ). One key way that miR-146a promotes repair is by modulating the polarization of microglia. Studies in EAE models demonstrate that overexpressing miR-146a enhances the anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype in microglia (Gudi et al. ; Zhang et al. ). These alternatively activated microglia contribute to tissue repair by phagocytosing damaged myelin debris, secreting growth factors that support OPC survival and differentiation, and producing anti-inflammatory cytokines that help resolve neuroinflammation. This establishes miR-146a as a master regulator of the reparative microenvironment (Gudi et al. ; Zhang et al. ) (Fig. ). Despite its anti-inflammatory classification, the functional efficacy of endogenous miR-146a in MS appears incomplete, as destructive inflammation persists despite its elevated expression (Chen et al. ). Several factors may contribute to this paradox, including interaction with competing signaling pathways, the presence of competing endogenous RNAs that bind to miR-146a, and nonlinear, dose-dependent effects on its target genes (Chen et al. ; Shu et al. ). The therapeutic window for miR-146a is consequently narrow because both insufficient and excessive expression can lead to dysfunctional outcomes (Shu et al. ). Further complexity arises from its close homology with the miR-146b isoform; therapeutic modulation of one may affect the other inadvertently (Paterson and Kriegel ). Additionally, the pleiotropic nature of miR-146a means that it regulates non-inflammatory targets, which can lead to adverse effects, such as apoptosis induction or synaptic dysfunction, in certain contexts (Mai et al. ). These findings collectively underscore the need for thorough and precise research to optimize any future miR-146a-based therapy. Critical future directions include conducting systematic dose-response studies to identify optimal expression levels, characterizing temporal requirements during different disease phases, and developing advanced delivery systems that can target specific cell populations. These refined approaches are essential to successfully harnessing the full therapeutic potential of modulating miR-146a while minimizing potential off-target effects in the treatment of demyelinating disorders (Paterson and Kriegel ; Quillet et al. ). The Impact of miR-146a on Remyelination and Glial Activation The influence of miR-146a on remyelination and glial cell behavior is complex and highly context-dependent, reflecting its role as a central molecular mediator in immune homeostasis and neuroinflammation. Functionally, miR-146a operates through intricate regulatory networks that primarily modulate neuroinflammatory processes and innate immune responses within the nervous system. These networks promote effects such as glial cell polarization toward anti-inflammatory phenotypes, neural regeneration, and myelination (Zhou et al. ; Tao et al. ) (Fig. ). Within the innate immune system, miR-146a acts as an essential negative feedback regulator. Its expression is induced by the activation of TLR signaling pathways, especially TLR4. Once expressed, miR-146a downregulates key adaptor molecules in the NF-κB pathway, including IRAK1 and TRAF6. This creates an autoregulatory loop that prevents uncontrolled inflammation while permitting a measured immune response (Doxaki et al. ). The importance of this regulation is evident in knockout models, in which the absence of miR-146a results in hyperresponsive macrophages, excessive cytokine production, and an inability to establish endotoxin tolerance (Boldin et al. ; Warrington et al. ). This regulatory function extends significantly into the CNS and is particularly relevant in MS. In EAE models, the therapeutic administration of miR-146a mimics has been shown to promote the polarization of microglia toward an anti-inflammatory M2 phenotype. This shift in glial activation promotes OPC differentiation and enhances remyelination, highlighting a clear reparative function (He et al. ). Additionally, in cases of bacterial encephalitis, miR-146a reduces neuroinflammatory responses in astrocytes by negatively regulating the TLR-mediated NF-κB pathway. This highlights its role in modulating glial activation across different cell types (Yang et al. ). However, evidence of potential detrimental effects counterbalances this ostensibly beneficial role. One study found that inflammatory microglia can transfer miR-146a to neurons via EVs. This transfer resulted in a significant decrease in dendritic spine and excitatory synapse density, leading to pathological synapse loss and neuronal dysfunction (Yang et al. ). The complexity of miR-146a is also evident in the adaptive immune system, where it acts as a safeguard against autoimmunity. In T cells, its expression increases with activation, and it is essential for maintaining immune tolerance in regulatory T cells (Tregs) (Yang et al. ; Romano et al. ). A deficiency in miR-146a can lead to spontaneous autoimmunity, which is characterized by dysregulated T and B cell responses, a loss of peripheral tolerance, and the production of pathological autoantibodies (Mehta and Baltimore ; Cho et al. ). In the context of MS, neuropathological studies show increased expression of miR-146a in active demyelinating lesions, with levels correlating with inflammatory activity. Elevated concentrations of miR-146a are also found in the CSF of patients during active disease (Wu et al. ; Morquette et al. ; Muñoz-San Martín et al. , ). Due to its ability to regulate multiple pathogenic processes, from inflammation to remyelination, the therapeutic potential of modulating miR-146a in neuroinflammatory disorders is significant (Wu et al. ; Muñoz-San Martín et al. , ). However, this potential is complicated by several challenging factors. Its mechanisms and effects vary substantially across different neurological conditions. Critical gaps remain in our understanding of optimal dosing, long-term effects, and potential off-target impacts on other tissues (Tao et al. ). Furthermore, the therapeutic window appears to be narrow because both insufficient and excessive expression can lead to dysfunctional outcomes. Its pleiotropic nature means that it regulates non-inflammatory targets, which can cause adverse effects, such as synaptic dysfunction or apoptosis, in certain contexts (Shu et al. ). Although miR-146a is a promising target due to its potent anti-inflammatory and pro-regenerative properties, its dualistic and context-dependent actions require a precise therapeutic approach. Future research should focus on systematic dose-response studies, detailed temporal mapping of its roles in different disease phases, and developing sophisticated delivery systems that can target specific cell populations in the CNS to safely harness its full therapeutic potential (Wu et al. ; Muñoz-San Martín et al. , ). Expression Profiles of miR-219 and miR-146a in MS Patients The expression patterns of miR-219 and miR-146a in MS patients demonstrate distinct and often compartment-specific trends in brain tissue, CSF, and blood, reflecting their diverse roles in disease pathophysiology. In brain tissue, miR-219 is significantly downregulated, particularly in white matter lesions of progressive forms of MS and in oligodendrocytes. Its crucial role in promoting differentiation and maintaining the mature myelin sheath is directly implicated in failed remyelination (Dugas et al. ; Tripathi et al. ; Duffy and McCoy ; Junker et al. ). This downregulation has also been observed in animal models of demyelination. Interestingly, delivering miR-219 has been shown to enhance remyelination, highlighting its potential as a therapeutic agent (Wang et al. , b). In contrast, the expression of miR-146a in the CNS is complex and cell-specific. It is often reported to be upregulated in active MS lesions, where it contributes to neuroinflammation by modulating immune responses (Muñoz-San Martín et al. , ). However, this trend is not uniform. Within astrocytes located in active lesions, for example, miR-146a appears to be downregulated, suggesting a limited role in lesion formation in that specific context (Junker et al. ; Rao et al. ). Additionally, miR-146a has been linked to promoting an anti-inflammatory state in microglia and reducing their numbers, suggesting a multifaceted function (Martin et al. ). The expression profiles of these miRNAs within the CSF provide insights into active disease processes. For miR-146a, however, findings are context-dependent. One study identified it as significantly downregulated in the CSF of MS patients compared to controls with other neurological diseases, suggesting it is part of an MS-specific miRNA signature (Quintana et al. ; Liu et al. , ). However, another study reported that miR-146a was upregulated in the CSF of MS patients with active gadolinium-enhancing lesions, suggesting that its expression may fluctuate with acute inflammatory activity (Muñoz-San Martín et al. , ). However, broader profiling studies of CSF in MS patients have not consistently identified either miR-219 or miR-146a as major differentially expressed biomarkers compared to other neurological conditions

This finding reflects the failure of remyelination processes within the central nervous system (Bruinsma et al. ). In peripheral blood and blood-derived samples, miR-146a is a significant and dynamic biomarker. It is often identified as part of miRNA signatures that distinguish MS subtypes in plasma, serum, and PBMCs. It frequently shows increased expression compared to controls, which reinforces its pro-inflammatory role (Junker et al. ; Quintana et al. ; Selmaj et al. ; Ghadiri et al. ; Amoruso et al. ). For example, a recent study found that miR-146a was significantly downregulated in the serum of patients with SPMS compared to patients with RRMS, suggesting its potential as a marker of disease progression (Al-Temaimi and Alroughani ). Its responsiveness to therapy is also notable; fingolimod treatment was shown to rapidly alter levels of miR-146a and other miRNAs in the extracellular vesicles of the serum of RRMS patients (Sáenz-Cuesta et al. ). However, contradictory results exist; some studies have noted both upregulation and downregulation, depending on the MS phase or treatments like natalizumab (Quintana et al. ; Freiesleben et al. ). In contrast, miR-219 has not been widely reported in peripheral blood-based studies in the reviewed literature, suggesting that its primary role and diagnostic value are likely more confined to CNS pathology. However, it is recognized as being enriched in pro-remyelination extracellular vesicles from animal models (Pusic and Kraig ; Mosora et al. ). These distinct and sometimes contrasting expression patterns across different biological compartments underscore the tissue-specific and context-dependent nature of miR-219 and miR-146a in MS (Table ). Synergistic Roles and Therapeutic Modulation of miR-219 and miR-146a in MS Emerging evidence reveals a sophisticated interplay between miR-219 and miR-146a in the pathophysiology of MS, where their concurrent deficiency in chronic lesions creates a vicious cycle of persistent inflammation and failed regeneration. These two miRNAs operate through complementary mechanisms: miR-219 acts as a master regulator of oligodendrocyte differentiation by directly targeting and suppressing key inhibitors of OPC maturation, such as PDGFRα, Sox6, and Zfp238 (Zhao et al. ; Dugas et al. ). Meanwhile, miR-146a primarily modulates neuroinflammation by regulating the NF-κB signaling pathway through targets such as IRAK1 and TRAF6 (Zhang et al. ; Wu et al. ; Fan et al. ). Under normal conditions, this dual regulatory system maintains a balanced microenvironment conducive to repair. However, in chronic MS, the loss of both functions leads to a synergistic blockade of remyelination. The absence of these miRNAs establishes multiple parallel pathological mechanisms. The absence of miR-219 regulation leads to sustained expression of differentiation inhibitors, which traps OPCs in a pre-myelinating state despite their adequate numbers in lesions (Shamaeizadeh and Mirian ). Concurrently, the loss of anti-inflammatory control by miR-146a leads to the uncontrolled activation of microglia and astrocytes through persistent NF-κB signaling. This generates a hostile, pro-inflammatory environment rich in reactive oxygen species (ROS) and cytotoxic cytokines, such as TNF-α and IL-6 (Fan et al. ; Perdaens and Pesch ). This environment fosters chronic glial activation, failed OPC differentiation, and progressive oxidative damage, which prevent repair and drive the progressive neurodegeneration characteristic of advanced MS. The result is a self-perpetuating cycle where inflammation inhibits repair and the lack of repair sustains inflammation. This mechanistic understanding establishes the strategic manipulation of miR-219 and miR-146a as a promising, dual-pronged therapeutic approach to interrupt this damaging cycle. Restoring miR-219 activity is a direct strategy for promoting remyelination. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that administering miR-219 mimics enhances OPC maturation and myelin repair in animal models while inhibiting astrocyte activation (Nguyen et al. ; Liu et al. , ). However, the therapeutic application of miR-146a requires a more nuanced approach given its complex biology. While its overexpression can promote an anti-inflammatory M2 microglial phenotype and reduce chronic neuroinflammation, its deficiency has paradoxically been observed to attenuate acute inflammatory responses and impair the capacity for endogenous remyelination (Zhang et al. ; Chen et al. ). Significant translational challenges must be overcome to advance these therapies. Developing efficient, targeted delivery systems that can cross the BBB and reach specific CNS cell populations remains a critical hurdle. Exosome-based platforms are promising candidates because of their natural capacity for miRNA transport and inherent biological compatibility Furthermore, the heterogeneity in miRNA expression across MS subtypes underscores the potential value of personalized therapeutic strategies, possibly guided by CSF miRNA profiling. Future research should focus on developing integrated treatment paradigms that address both miR-219-mediated remyelination and miR-146a-regulated inflammation while establishing robust monitoring systems to evaluate efficacy. A comprehensive approach targeting both miR-219 and miR-146a has the potential to significantly advance MS therapeutics. This strategy simultaneously promotes OPC differentiation and modulates the inflammatory microenvironment, addressing both the neurodegenerative and inflammatory components of the disease. Successful clinical translation of this dual-targeted approach could catalyze a paradigm shift in MS treatment by moving beyond symptomatic management toward genuine neurorestorative intervention. Current Challenges in miRNA-Based Therapeutics for Multiple Sclerosis Translating miRNA research into viable clinical applications for MS is a promising yet formidable endeavor that faces a multifaceted array of scientific, technical, and safety-related challenges. One primary obstacle arises in the discovery phase, where identifying reliable miRNA targets is often hindered by studies utilizing relatively small patient cohorts. These limited sample sizes may not represent the broader MS population adequately, creating uncertainty about the diagnostic and therapeutic relevance of candidate miRNAs in diverse clinical settings (Zabalza et al. ). This underscores the urgent need for large-scale, multicenter validation studies and comprehensive meta-analyses to distinguish genuinely promising miRNA targets from potential false positives that can arise in smaller investigations (Ho et al. ). Beyond identification, effectively delivering therapeutic miRNA modulators to the CNS is a monumental hurdle. The BBB acts as a formidable gatekeeper, requiring the development of sophisticated delivery systems to sufficiently penetrate the tissue and target MS pathology (Wu et al. ). Although research into nanoparticle platforms and targeted mechanisms is ongoing, substantial optimization is still needed for clinical application. This challenge is further complicated by a critical lack of technical standardization across the field. Considerable variability in sample processing protocols, analysis methodologies, and data interpretation between laboratories makes it difficult to compare results and slows collective progress (Felekkis and Papaneophytou ). Key areas requiring urgent standardization include normalization techniques for miRNA quantification, uniform protocols for miRNA isolation, and the establishment of standardized reference materials for assay calibration (Precazzini et al. ). Safety considerations present another significant challenge. The pleiotropic nature of miRNAs, whereby a single miRNA can regulate hundreds of mRNA targets, raises legitimate concerns about off-target effects and unintended biological consequences following therapeutic modulation (Galvão-Lima et al. ). Therefore, comprehensive preclinical testing is essential to characterize the potential immunogenicity, toxicity, stability, and long-term effects of any miRNA-based intervention (Pagoni et al. ). The complexity of miRNA regulatory networks, in which individual mRNAs can be regulated by multiple miRNAs, further complicates safety assessments and therapeutic design. The development of miRNA biomarkers faces challenges related to standardization and validation. Discrepancies in biofluid sources (e.g., plasma versus serum), sample collection methods, anticoagulant use, and storage conditions can substantially impact miRNA profiles and complicate cross-study comparisons (Felekkis et al. ; Chorley et al. ). The analytical phase introduces additional complexities, including the lack of universally accepted reference genes for normalization and the need for disease-specific endogenous controls that account for variability in different pathological states (Pagoni et al. ). Current limitations also include technical difficulties in quantifying small miRNAs, an incomplete understanding of their biological functions, and potential matrix interference in clinical samples (Bottani et al. ). The proposed solutions to advance the field are multifaceted. These solutions include implementing multiple reference genes and spike-in controls, strictly adhering to standardized protocols, organizing large multicenter validation studies, and developing comprehensive research guidelines (O’Brien et al. ; Wang et al. ). Future research must prioritize the following: establishing international consensus protocols, developing disease-specific miRNA panels, engineering improved delivery systems, and conducting comprehensive safety studies. Despite the many challenges, circulating miRNAs continue to show great promise as diagnostic tools and therapeutic agents for MS. Their

The next decade will be pivotal in translating these molecular discoveries into clinical applications. Future Perspectives and Roadmap for Clinical Translation The future management of MS is poised for a transformative shift toward a more precise, equitable, and holistic approach. A critical initial step in this process is the global validation and refinement of diagnostic criteria. The upcoming revision of the McDonald criteria should incorporate data from diverse international populations, not just the primarily Caucasian groups on which they were originally based. There should be a particular focus on non-Western European and low-prevalence regions (Thompson et al. ). To improve accessibility, particularly in settings with limited resources, the integration of cost-effective serological biomarkers is anticipated. Simultaneously, it is crucial to address the significant global disparities in access to high-efficacy DMTs. This will require coordinated strategies to increase public awareness, educate health officials, and establish transparent procurement processes involving neurologists and patient advocacy groups (Rivera and Macias ). The growing importance of follow-on medications and biosimilars requires robust clinical data to ensure their long-term efficacy and safety (Steinberg et al. ). At the core of this evolution is the realization of the full potential of precision medicine, which is driven by the integration of advanced technologies (University of California et al. 2016; Schinocca et al. ; Fox ). Developing a rapid learning healthcare system integrated with electronic health records that is constantly updated with new prognostic features will be essential for deploying dynamic clinical decision support tools (Liu et al. ). This data-driven approach will pave the way for combination therapies that target multiple immune pathways simultaneously, offering superior efficacy and reducing the risk of treatment resistance compared to single-target approaches (Pitt et al. ; Krysko et al. ). Successful implementation of these strategies hinges on robust collaboration between academic institutions, pharmaceutical companies, and bioinformatics groups to validate biomarkers in large, longitudinal cohorts (Gauthier et al. ; Cree et al. ). A particularly promising area of research lies in developing miRNA-based therapies. The clinical translation of candidates such as the pro-remyelinating miR-219 and the immunomodulatory miR-146a critically depends on overcoming delivery challenges to the CNS. Advanced nanocarriers, such as low-immunogenicity exosomes, and engineered synthetic nanoparticles show promise in protecting therapeutic miRNAs and facilitating their transport across the BBB (Osorio-Querejeta et al. ; Briuglia et al. ; Yang and Lai ; Pan et al. ). Exosomes loaded with miR-219, for instance, have already demonstrated enhanced remyelination in experimental models delivering miR-146a have effectively modulated autoimmunity (Osorio-Querejeta et al. ; Pan et al. ). The future of MS care will ultimately be defined by a collaborative, patient-centric model. Active involvement from patient societies is crucial to aligning outcomes with patient-identified needs and improving health literacy (Alper ). A holistic management paradigm that proactively addresses comorbidities and promotes healthy lifestyles is integral to improving long-term global outcomes (Kowalec et al. ). Uniting global diagnostic standardization, equitable access, data-driven precision medicine, innovative therapeutics, and the patient voice will enable the field to successfully transition from a one-size-fits-all approach to a future of mechanistically tailored, effective, and accessible care for every individual with MS. MicroRNA Delivery Strategies in Multiple Sclerosis The successful implementation of miRNA-based therapeutics for MS is fundamentally constrained by the need for advanced delivery platforms that can overcome formidable biological obstacles (Zabalza et al. ). Unprotected miRNA molecules undergo rapid enzymatic degradation in the bloodstream and exhibit minimal penetration across the highly selective BBB, necessitating the development of sophisticated nanocarriers for effective transport to sites of pathology within the CNS (Figueroa et al. ). Current research efforts focus on a variety of delivery systems ranging from synthetic constructs, such as liposomes and polymeric nanoparticles, to biologically derived vehicles, such as exosomes. Due to their inherent biocompatibility, low immunogenicity, and natural ability to cross the BBB as part of intercellular communication, exosomes, which are natural extracellular vesicles, have emerged as a particularly promising candidate. Their therapeutic potential has been demonstrated by research showing successful miRNA delivery. For example, studies have shown that extracellular vesicles loaded with miR-219a-5p, a key regulator of oligodendrocyte maturation, are more effective than synthetic counterparts at crossing the BBB and stimulating OPC differentiation. The clinical relevance of this approach was confirmed by intranasal administration in an EAE model, which led to a significant improvement in disease scores (Osorio-Querejeta et al. ). Further supporting the reparative role of this pathway, serum exosomes isolated from environmentally enriched animals, which carry substantially elevated levels of miR-219, were shown to promote OPC maturation and enhance myelination within damaged lesions (Pusic and Kraig ). Exosomes’ versatility also allows for the delivery of multi-miRNA cocktails. For example, exosomes derived from interferon-γ-stimulated dendritic cells have been loaded with a combination of miRNAs, including miR-219, miR-451, miR-181a, and miR-665. These miRNAs synergistically drive OPC differentiation and remyelination (Pusic et al. ). In addition to the reparative strategy focused on miR-219, regulating miR-146a offers another way to reduce the inflammation that causes MS. The dysregulation of miR-146a, a master regulator of innate immunity in MS patients, solidifies its status as a promising therapeutic target (Giuliani et al. ). Although dedicated delivery studies for miR-146a are limited, several platforms demonstrate significant promise. For example, engineered exosomes derived from bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells have been shown to effectively deliver immunomodulatory miRNAs and improve disease outcomes in EAE models by targeting pathways that activate microglia (Fan et al. ). The natural role of exosomes as shuttles for regulatory miRNAs provides a robust rationale for their use (Mohammadinasr et al. ). Alongside this method, synthetic nanocarriers offer a highly customizable alternative. Cationic liposomes and polymers, including polyethyleneimine (PEI), effectively condense and shield miRNA molecules. However, refinements like PEGylation are often necessary to mitigate inherent toxicity, enhance circulatory stability, and improve target specificity (Briuglia et al. ; Yang and Lai ). A notably innovative, non-viral approach utilizes engineered, bacteriophage-based MS2 VLPs. In a pivotal study, MS2 VLPs were loaded with miR-146a and equipped with cell-penetrating peptides, which facilitated efficient cellular delivery and resulted in significant inhibition of autoantibody production in a lupus-prone mouse model. This finding is directly relevant to MS. The low immunogenicity and cytotoxicity of this VLP system position it as a leading candidate for RNA therapy delivery in CNS autoimmune conditions (Pan et al. ). Continued refinement of a diverse arsenal of nanocarriers, including natural exosomes, synthetic polymers, and engineered VLPs, is a critical frontier in advancing precision medicine for MS. These delivery systems are indispensable for realizing the clinical potential of therapeutic miRNAs by ensuring their efficient, targeted delivery to CNS lesions. By safeguarding their molecular cargo and enabling transit across the BBB, these sophisticated technologies hold immense promise for addressing the dual pathological pillars of MS concurrently: fostering neural repair and suppressing detrimental neuroinflammation (Table ). Conclusion The evolving landscape of MS therapeutics is witnessing a paradigm shift from purely immunosuppressive strategies toward interventions that address neuroinflammation and facilitate CNS repair concurrently. The synergistic targeting of miR-219 and miR-146a exemplifies this innovative approach, offering a biologically nuanced strategy to disrupt the vicious cycle of demyelination and inflammatory neurodegeneration. Due to its role in regulating the progression of the oligodendrocyte lineage, activating miR-219 provides a direct way to reverse myelin loss. Meanwhile, the modulation of miR-146a in different contexts provides critical control over detrimental neuroimmune activation. However, successfully translating this dual-targeting paradigm into clinical practice requires overcoming significant challenges. These include developing sophisticated delivery platforms that can traverse the BBB with cellular precision, comprehensively mapping the dose-response relationships and temporal dynamics of miRNAs across disease stages, and identifying robust biomarkers for patient stratification and therapeutic monitoring. Future research should prioritize engineering next-generation nanocarriers, such as engineered exosomes and virus-like particles, and implementing combinatorial regimens that integrate miRNA-based agents with conventional DMTs.
